body: On Tuesday, I published a story about how YouTube appeared to be testing hiding the dislike button on videos, with at least two users on X sharing screenshots of the dislike button moved into the three-dot menu. But a YouTube spokesperson, in a Wednesday statement to The Verge, confirmed that YouTube is “not testing hiding the dislike button on YouTube for users.”
YouTube says it isn’t testing hiding the dislike button
YouTube creators, on their own videos, will have the dislike button moved behind the three-dot menu, but that’s not the case for regular users.
However, YouTube is introducing a new UI for creators on their uploaded videos where the dislike button will be moved.
Here’s the full statement, from spokesperson Kimberly Taylor:

We are not testing hiding the dislike button on YouTube for users. We’re introducing a new UI for creators on their own uploaded videos, where dislike is behind the three-dot menu, and as always, they can find their full dislike counts in Studio, alongside other analytics.
The new UI is rolling out to creators in “the coming weeks,” Taylor says.

The change for creators follows past adjustments to the dislike button on the platform. YouTube hid the public dislike count on videos starting in 2021 as a way to prevent harassment, and it removed the dislike button video from Shorts earlier this year.

articles.headline: Goal, assist... goal-kick - Kane underlines Ballon d'Or credentials
keyFacts: Harry Kane delivered a strong performance during Bayern Munich's 2-2 draw with Arsenal in the Champions League.
Kane scored a penalty and contributed an assist, bringing his career tally of goals against Arsenal to 16.
The winner of the Ballon d'Or, for which Kane is considered a frontrunner, will be announced on Monday.
body: - Published
Even by Harry Kane's remarkable standards, this was mightily impressive.

There were fewer than 25 minutes on the clock during Bayern Munich's thrilling 2-2 draw with Arsenal in the Champions League when the forward took matters into his own hands in a bid to break the deadlock.
As the Premier League champions prepared to defend a Bayern goal-kick, Kane seized the initiative by launching his side up the pitch with a raking 80-yard pass.
It was a moment of remarkable ingenuity from the England international, one that almost ended with Bayern taking the lead.
"Under Vincent Kompany, he has been given a level of trust that he has probably never had before under any other manager," former Manchester City defender Nedum Onuoha told BBC Sport.
"For all the things we've seen him do and the positions we've seen him roam into, nobody has seen him take a goal-kick before.

"But even someone like Manuel Neuer, who is his senior and has been at Bayern for a large part of his career, sees Harry Kane put the ball down and thinks, 'OK, sure'. He lets Harry go for it because he thinks whatever he sees is going to be correct.
"At the same time, there were Bayern players running forward because they knew that the ball could come.

"For him to be taking a goal-kick is not something you may want to see very often. You don't necessarily want your number nine to be THAT deep, but the nature of his game when he is playing for Bayern is to roam, and today it was a huge benefit to the team."
Although Kane was denied the opportunity to add another outstanding assist to his already impressive catalogue, he did not have to wait long to make another decisive contribution.
After Eberechi Eze had put Arsenal ahead, Kane helped Bayern restore parity, bending a sumptuous pass around Jurrien Timber for Alphonso Davies to finish.
The England captain then fired the hosts in front from the penalty spot midway through the second half, taking his career tally of goals against Arsenal to 16.
But Declan Rice struck late on to earn Arsenal a share of the spoils.
'When you play against him, you see how much of a pain it is'
For Kane, it was another mesmerising performance that underlined his credentials as the frontrunner for the 2026 Ballon d'Or.

The former Tottenham Hotspur captain, 33, could become the first Englishman since Michael Owen in 2001 to win the prestigious individual award, with Barcelona's Lamine Yamal and Paris St-Germain forward and current holder Ousmane Dembele among the favourites.
Kane was named on the 30-man shortlist in September, with the winner due to be announced on Monday following a vote by an international jury of 100 journalists.
"He is the clear winner. His numbers speak for themselves. The year he has had has been remarkable," Arsenal and England midfielder Declan Rice told TNT Sports.
"When you play with him, you realise how good he is, and when you play against him, you see how much of a pain it is.
"He is ridiculous, such a good player, and I am lucky I can play with him, not so lucky I have to play against him."
By scoring against Arsenal on Wednesday night, Kane became only the second player in Champions League history to find the net in 10 consecutive matches.
The only other player to achieve the feat was five-time Ballon d'Or winner Cristiano Ronaldo, who scored in 11 successive matches for Real Madrid between June 2017 and April 2018.

"Kane certainly looks at home at Bayern. He understands the team and its system, and they all understand him. They know that when he gets the ball at his feet, wherever that may be, something good can happen," Onuoha added.
"I think all the Bayern players are really playing into that, but then Harry steps up and scores a penalty as well.

"Having freedom is probably the best way to describe what he has got playing for Bayern, because he will work hard defensively, which allows him the freedom to be creative when he is in attack. For now, he certainly is thriving."
Kane's goal against Arsenal took his tally to 156 in 158 appearances since joining Bayern Munich from Tottenham in 2023.
It was another night to remember for the England captain, but the best could yet be to come, with the Ballon d'Or ceremony in London looming.
"It would be amazing to win," said Kane afterwards. "The voting closed a long time ago so there's nothing I can do, just wait and see what happens."

articles.headline: Mark Zuckerberg says Meta is 'entering a new phase' with Muse
keyFacts: CEO Mark Zuckerberg said Meta is shifting to a scaling phase for its Muse agent after reaching over 10 million users since September.
Zuckerberg stated that Meta plans to monetize Muse through business transaction fees, commerce tools, and AI subscriptions.
Zuckerberg predicted that Muse will eventually generate higher revenue per user than Meta's existing apps like Facebook and Instagram.
body: Mark Zuckerberg says Meta is 'entering a new phase' with Muse
He expects the agent will generate more revenue per user than the company's apps.

It's only been a few weeks since Meta introduced Muse, but the company's personal agent is already becoming central to Meta's plan to start making money off its massive investment in AI. CEO Mark Zuckerberg said that the company is already working on monetizing the agent, and that he expects Muse to eventually generate more revenue per user than Facebook and Instagram.

Even though Muse is only available in the US and Canada, Meta has already seen significant adoption of the agent. Zuckerberg said that more than 10 million people have started using it since its early September rollout. "Now that Muse has clear product market fit, we are entering a new phase and a more operational phase that is focused on scaling it," Zuckerberg said during the company's third-quarter earnings call Wednesday. "We expect to grow Muse to serve billions of people."

Muse is also significantly more expensive for Meta to operate compared with its other services, and Zuckerberg said the company was already working on its plans to monetize the agent. Meta plans to build "commerce tools" that will allow it to charge businesses fees for transactions facilitated by its agent, the CEO said. He noted that shopping is currently the "most common" use case for the agent, and that people are spending an average of $200 per purchase with Muse. Meta will incorporate its AI subscriptions for people and business owners who use the agent more heavily as well.

Zuckerberg predicted that revenue from Muse could eventually surpass the money it currently makes from its apps, at least by some metrics. "The average revenue per American user for our existing family of apps users is several hundreds of dollars annually, and we expect that Muse will reach an even higher level over time due to the amount of commerce that we already see taking place," Zuckerberg said.

Muse is also "central" to Meta's plans to make more money from its AI glasses, according to Zuckerberg. While the company doesn't currently "make a large profit on the hardware" it sells, adding Muse to the product will help Meta sell more AI subscriptions, Zuckerberg predicted.

Meta previewed Muse on its smart glasses last month during Connect. The company said users will be able to talk to their agent in much the same way they can currently chat with Meta AI, and will be able to check in on tasks or add items to their agent's to-do list. Meta didn't specify if Muse on its glasses would require a separate subscription, but Zuckerberg's statements suggest that at least some Muse features will be paywalled on the glasses. (The company has contemplated upcharging for other glasses features, including its upcoming hearing enhancement ability.) Muse will be available on Meta's glasses "next month," Zuckerberg said.

articles.headline: Russia released a US prisoner. What did they get out of it?
keyFacts: Russia released 74-year-old American prisoner Stephen Hubbard to the United States on Wednesday.
President Donald Trump claimed the US gave nothing in return for the release out of respect for him.
The Trump administration recently waived economic sanctions on Russia, struck a diesel deal, and interrupted US intelligence sharing with Ukraine.
body: Donald Trump speaks during an RNC fundraising event at Mar-a-Lago on October 16, 2026. | Eric Lee/Getty Images
This story appeared in The Logoff , a daily newsletter that helps you stay informed about the Trump administration without letting political news take over your life. Subscribe here .
Welcome to The Logoff: President Donald Trump is cozying up to Russia again.

What’s happening? On Wednesday, Russia released an American prisoner , 74-year-old retired teacher Stephen Hubbard, back to the US. The US, Trump said in a social media post, “out of respect for President Trump, was not required to give anything in return.”

Hubbard’s release is unquestionably good news. But Trump is wrong: In just the last month, his administration has delivered for Russia in more ways than one, often inexplicably and despite bipartisan condemnation.

What is Trump doing for Russia? Late last week, he waived upcoming economic sanctions on Russia that he had only recently signed into law after they passed Congress with overwhelming bipartisan support. He also:
Struck a diesel deal with Russia, temporarily lifting fuel sanctions on the country in exchange for Russia releasing a trivial amount of diesel into the global market;
Announced — seemingly without talking to either party — a Russia-Ukraine “energy ceasefire” favorable to Russia (which has since fallen apart);
Temporarily interrupted US intel sharing with Ukraine and played a role in interfering with Ukraine’s access to Starlink, which helps power the country’s drone warfare against Russia; and
Called on Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to be replaced .
Last month, Trump also invited Russian President Vladimir Putin to the annual G20 summit later this year, which would mark Putin’s first appearance since 2019.

What does Trump get out of all of this? There’s Hubbard’s release, but taking that on Trump’s own terms ( muddled though they are), the US didn’t give anything to secure it — which means that all of those favors have amounted to not much at all, other than papering over Russia’s role as an international bad actor and breaking with US allies in Europe.

Why does this matter? Trump’s Russia embrace comes at an awful time for Ukraine, which, as the New York Times reported earlier this month, is facing a Russian campaign to “freeze Ukrainians into submission” as winter approaches. Nevertheless, on Wednesday, Trump envoy Steve Witkoff called Putin a “humanitarian.”
And with that, it’s time to log off…

I was delighted to learn about the US’s new national park yesterday, its 64th. Chiricahua National Park — until Tuesday, only a national monument — is the first new park in six years. Located in southeastern Arizona, it’s also called the “Wonderland of Rocks,” according to the Washington Post ; you can read more about it here with a gift link.
Have a great evening, and we’ll see you back here tomorrow!

articles.headline: Ryan Bertrand leads consortium to make £87m investment in EFL club
keyFacts: Former England defender Ryan Bertrand is leading a consortium proposing an £87m minority investment in League One club AFC Wimbledon.
The proposed deal involves Sloane Street Capital paying £16m for 34 per cent of shares initially, followed by £71m over five years.
AFC Wimbledon's fan owners in the Dons Trust will vote by November 17 on whether to approve the proposal.
body: Former England defender Ryan Bertrand is leading a consortium proposing a £87m minority investment in AFC Wimbledon.
Bertrand enjoyed a 17-year career playing for the likes of Chelsea , Southampton and Aston Villa , and is now at the forefront of a group looking to acquire a stake in the League One side.
Ryan Bertrand made 262 Premier League appearances in his career Getty
The former full-back has teamed up with British technology expert Omar Mir, who is the sole funder of the proposed minority share buyout through investment vehicle Sloane Street Capital (SSC).
In a complicated deal, SSC are looking to pay £16m for approximately 34 per cent of the club’s shares this season.
They then plan to invest a further £71m over the next five years, at which point SSC would own 90 per cent of the club’s economic value.
AFC Wimbledon are owned by supporters in the form of the 6,265-strong Dons Trust, who currently own 50.01 per cent of the voting shares at the club – designed to ensure it remains fan-controlled.
After the Dons Trust board presented SSC’s proposal to its members on Wednesday night, they will now vote on whether to accept it.

For the proposal to be approved, a 75 per cent majority is needed, with at least 50 per cent of the members voting, and that majority must account for at least 40 per cent of the total membership, with voting closing on November 17.
If the deal is successful, SSC would oversee football operations, led by Bertrand as senior football advisor, but work within budgets and processes agreed by the AFCW PLC board.
The move would also see two of SSC’s minority shareholders, investment fund boss Stuart Fiertz and sports executive Oliver Ward, joining the club’s board.
Bertrand: Wimbledon role would be an ‘honour’
Bertrand, who won the Champions League , FA Cup and Europa League with Chelsea, recently discussed his hopes of being involved at Plough Lane.
He said: “AFC Wimbledon’s story is unique in English football and it was built by its supporters. We felt at home from our very first meetings.
Bertrand started in Chelsea’s 2012 Champions League final victory over Bayern Munich Getty
Plough Lane has been home to AFC Wimbledon since 2020 Getty
“We are not here to change what this club is. We are here to help it go further on and off the pitch, for the men’s team, the women’s team and the academy.
“It would be an honour to join the Wimbledon family and help write the next chapter, and we look forward to meeting members and answering their questions over the coming weeks.”
Under the terms of the proposed deal, the Dons Trust voting rights would be unaffected.
They would hold veto control of the Plough Lane – known as the Cherry Red Record Stadium sponsorship reasons – freehold.
Other ideas floated as part of the potential investment include SSC taking two of the 12 seats on the club board, as well as an observer position.
Meanwhile, the Dons Trust would retain veto over the club’s name, badge, colours, ground and constitution.
AFC Wimbledon are currently 16th in League One Getty
If SSC were to sell its stake, the Dons Trust would have first refusal and could block anyone they deem unsuitable investors.
Also included in the terms of a potential deal, SSC would see its share of AFC Wimbledon’s value would stop growing immediately in the event of the consortium missing a payment.
Control would then return to the club within three months.
Earlier this year, the Dons Trust voted in favour of external investment as long as fan ownership and control were protected.
Since then, the board has considered more than 20 potential investors, with SSC emerging as the strongest.
As for Bertrand, should a deal transpire, this would represent his first venture into club ownership after retiring from football at Leicester in 2023.
Bertrand was capped 19 times by England, and is looking to move into football at board level Getty

Angus Fox, chair of the Dons Trust board, said of SSC’s proposal: “The deal brings at least £87million into AFC Wimbledon over five years, while the Trust keeps a permanent majority of the votes, control of the Plough Lane freehold and a veto over everything that makes us who we are.
“We have set out the factors to weigh as plainly as the opportunities.
“The board recommends a yes vote, but this is our members’ club and our members’ decision.”

articles.headline: Your Favorite Video Games Will Always Be Influenced By Manga
keyFacts: The Brooklyn Museum in New York City is hosting the Art of Manga exhibit, curated by Nicole Coolidge Rousmaniere, from October 3, 2026, to January 31, 2027.
The exhibition features works from 10 prominent manga artists, including Jiro Taniguchi, Rumiko Takahashi, Eiichiro Oda, and Hirohiko Araki.
The article highlights how manga heavily influences video games, noting specific connections to titles like Persona, Dark Souls, and Yakuza: Like a Dragon.
body: In the heart of Brooklyn, there is now a devastatingly gorgeous manga panel from Jiro Taniguchi's Ice Age: Chronicle of the Earth hung on a gallery wall. I can't tell you what it says--I fear my scant familiarity with Japanese doesn't extend to literacy in kanji--but I can tell you what it portrays: a cityscape consumed by nature. A lush tangle of vines and trees reclaiming the Earth from its disastrous, mettlesome inheritors.

While I doubt this panel and manga are the first time this kind of image has cropped up, it certainly feels like a progenitor to many similar visuals across the years. Your mind might jump to I Am Legend, the Will Smith-led feature film about a post-apocalyptic New York City, for example. My mind jumped straight to Nier Automata's city that's been lost to time, as well as The Last of Us' many dilapidated small towns and US metropolises. Though I went into the Brooklyn Museum's new Art of Manga exhibit already curious about what connections the form might have to games, it became quickly apparent that manga has always been in conversation with other mediums, influencing everything from anime to gaming.

The Brooklyn Museum, located right near Prospect Park in New York City, is currently home to the Art of Manga exhibit. Curated by Nicole Coolidge Rousmaniere--whose love of manga stems from early exposure to French graphic novels and reading Astro Boy at a seminal age--the gallery features a beautiful selection of Taniguchi’s work, as well as select other notable mangaka (manga artists and authors) of outsized influence. This includes Rumiko Takahashi, best known for her work on Ranma ½ and Inuyasha, Eiichiro Oda, the renowned creator of One Piece, and Hirohiko Araki, whose gorgeously styled illustrations from Jojo’s Bizarre Adventure are among the exhibits crown jewels.

In total, the exhibit draws from the work of 10 mangaka , evenly split between male and female authors of varying popularity and prefectures of Japan, and explores different kinds of subject matter including inner-city living and queer life. This was essential to Rousmaniere, As she explained, "If I had featured fewer artists, the exhibition would not have been as powerful; We might not have gotten across the incredible range of these artists and the power of the line that they employ." The Art of Manga exhibit, evidently, needed to be big.

And big it is. At its center, there is a reading room with bookshelves full of manga related to the artists spotlighted in the exhibit. Whole walls are adorned with iconic illustrations of some of the manga (a particularly poignant scene from One Piece comes to mind near the exhibit's end), but some of the highlighted art is also quite grand. Jojo's Bizarre Adventure, for example, is the subject of what Rousmaniere calls "the heart of the exhibition:" a 12-panel composition called "There is always a Traitor." The work consists of a series of life-sized panels of Jojo’s Bizarre Adventure’s Stand users assembled in tableau, with each panel towering over the average visitor and making the cast out to be even larger than life than they typically are. Or as Rousmaniere puts it, Araki's "2D figures are in fact 3D, and jump from the page into our imagination."

"What I adore about Araki Hirohiko is his versatility and his ability to embrace new challenges, be it life-size painting or lithography, fashion, or music. He has no bounds on his imagination and I think this is what makes him and his work so vital," Rousmaniere extolled.

A little ways away from that massive installation is a smaller piece from Araki that might look strikingly similar to many gamers. In it, many characters from Jojo's Bizarre Adventure stand huddled up on what appears to be a bus. The distinct juxtaposition of the cast's bright colors and exotic patterns against the drab gray of the bus interior cuts an imposing image. To the eye of your average RPG player, like me, the ensemble might look eerily close to that of a Persona game.

If you’re anything like me, you probably can’t look at Araki’s work without immediately drawing connections to Persona , a beloved RPG series from Atlus that touts, among many other things, an impeccable sense of forward-thinking fashion and style on par with the closets of characters like Jotaro and Jolyne.

But that’s not all they have in common. The two also share a penchant for the supernatural and mythological, and both casts can summon powerful beings in battle. In the manga of JJBA, these forces are known as Stands, but in the world of Persona, they are called … well, Persona. The creators of the Persona games have never outright confirmed the influence of JJBA on the production of the series, but their lineage feels like an unspoken truth.

Manga's influence on games doesn't begin or end there, either. The mangaka of Dragon Ball, the late Akira Toriyama, literally helped sculpt the visual identity of both the Dragon Quest series and Chrono Trigger, two early successes for the companies that were then known separately as Square and Enix. Beyond that, it feels like the sensibilities and attitudes of these games and that era of RPG--the fascination with small-town living and domesticity for example--owe something to the genial nature of Toriyama's characters and the warm fantasy tapestry he helped to create.

Alternatively, much later RPGs feel like direct descendants of Berserk, the late Kentaro Miura’s manga, which has been a huge influence in the rise of dark fantasy. Miura's bleak fantasy epic has long served as a muse of sorts for a whole class of character in the Final Fantasy series, and has also been a major touchstone for From Software’s oeuvre like Dark Souls and Elden Ring.

Of course, manga has also paved the way for anime, which often reimagines and reinterprets manga and has made global phenomena of many works, such as One Piece. One Piece has become one of the best-known brands since its anime adaptation enraptured the world, and now there are One Piece nights at baseball games! I can’t walk to one of my local trains without seeing a plush of Chopper in a neighbor’s window or a straw-hat ornament on a passerby's bag. And when you see Oda’s art on display in Brooklyn Museum’s exhibit, including an illustration that explicitly features Nami and Usopp playing video games featuring some very familiar caricatures, it’s easy to see why the series and its cast have inspired such awe across the world and artistic mediums.

The camaraderie between Luffy and his friends, which serves as the emotional core of the series, is aspirational and has seemingly served as the template for one of gaming’s more recent band of oddities. In an interview with Crunchyroll , the newest head of Ryu Ga Gotoku Studio (and longtime writer) Masayoshi Yokoyama admitted that the cast of Yakuza: Like a Dragon, the game that transformed the brawler series into a turn-based RPG, was molded after Luffy and the Straw Hat Pirates.

Yokoyama told Crunchyroll at the time, "To me, Ichiban is basically Luffy. And around him there’s Zoro and Nami and basically the rest of the party, you know? One Piece’s party composition was on my mind so much during writing that it was a massive influence." It feels like Yokoyama's only scratching the surface with that comparison too. As two long-running series that often painstakingly shift perspectives to illuminate struggles against unfair systems and institutions, I don’t think it’s the only way that the two are alike.

Even if it is indirect, or I guess roundabout in this case, manga's force has become increasingly undeniable over the years. Rousmaniere shared, "When I was in Japan in the '80s, everyone was reading manga. I was studying archaeology and the archaeologists mostly all read manga. Manga captures the zeitgeist of a moment that other forms do not in a tangible, and not fleeting, fashion." As it's bled into anime with increasing success, manga's influence has only grown. Now it is, per Rousmaniere, "in Barnes and Noble in the US, in Waterstones in the UK, and in airports around the country." It's everywhere.

Though the Art of Manga exhibit may not overtly draw attention to the forms’ ties to games, there is one outstanding reference to the modern gaming landscape that’s hard to ignore. Before you enter the exhibit, right outside the entrance to Brooklyn Museum’s gift shop that is now itself adorned with manga-inspired merch and paraphernalia, there is an army of gashapon ("gacha") machines that visitors are encouraged to play. I clocked everything from Digimon to My Hero Academia and more among the capsule-sized toys and charms that players could pull.

"Many people watch gamers just as I enjoy watching visitors and museum workers choosing their gashapon at the front of the store," Rousmaniere shared, drawing an interesting line from her enjoyment of seeing people turn their fascination with manga into a literal keepsake to how one might enjoy watching a streamer try pulling a legendary roll in a gacha game like Genshin Impact. That gashapon machines, whose mechanics have become the basis for countless popular video games in the last decade, just so happen to be halfway between manga and gaming makes their prominent inclusion here quite serendipitous.

My big takeaway from the Art of Manga exhibit? Art goes beyond frames and borders, touches other artists and mediums outside of itself all the time, and continues spreading regardless of genres, nations, or any other manner of restraint. In some ways, you can draw an incredibly clear line from manga to games, like Araki's work and something like Persona. In other ways, the influence might be felt but not obviously seen. But it's always worth exploring other forms and, for instance, walking through a gallery like this one and interrogating where it all might stem from.
Brooklyn Museum's Art of Manga exhibit runs from October 3, 2026 to January 31, 2027.

articles.headline: Democrats have 11-point lead among likely voters as Trump’s approval rating craters – live
keyFacts: Likely voters prefer Democratic candidates over Republicans by 11 percentage points, according to New York Times and Siena University polling.
A New Mexico judge ordered Meta to pay a $25 billion penalty after a jury found it deceived users about data privacy.
Donald Trump will continue his campaign blitz in South Carolina for Republican Senate nominee Darline Graham before the midterm elections.
body: Democrats have 11-point lead among likely voters as Trump’s approval rating craters – live
New poll finds likely voters prefer Democratic candidates over Republicans running for office by 11 percentage points; Trump campaigns in South Carolina
New polling shows likely voters prefer Democratic candidates over Republicans, fewer than two weeks until midterm elections
New polling from the New York Times and Siena University shows that likely voters prefer Democratic candidates over Republicans running for office by 11 percentage points.
Meanwhile, Donald Trump’s approval rating dropped to a new low for this particular survey – 36%.

Notably, according to the Times’ polling, the perception of either party has shifted over the last two years. The number of people who consider Democrats as the party of the working class has grown by five points – from 48% to 53%, while it’s dropped by five points for Republicans – from 45% to 40%.
Musk threatens to 'come for' Democrats who 'pick fights' with him in new Congress
Elon Musk – the tech billionaire, Trump ally, and founder of Tesla and Space X – has threatened to home in on Democrats who pursue him in the next Congress.

“Live by the sword, die by the sword,” Musk wrote on X, the social media platform he bought in 2022. “Those who pick fights with me should understand that I will find out who is really pulling the strings and come for them, not just their puppets.”

This comes after Politico reported earlier today that Democratic lawmakers were considering how best to investigate Musk, and his businesses, if the party gains control of Congress following the midterm elections.

US envoy Steve Witkoff announced this morning that Russia authorities had freed Stephen Hubbard, the first American known to be convicted of fighting as a mercenary in Ukraine. Hubbard was arrested when the Russians briefly took over the Ukrainian city of Izium at the start of the ongoing conflict in 2022.

Donald Trump welcomed the news,noting the prisoner release was the result of a direct request he made to Putin in a telephone call last week. Meanwhile, after Witkoff’s discussions with Putin in St Petersburg, he flattered the Russian president by calling him a “humanitarian”. The emissary’s comments drew bipartisan backlash, but Trump defended them: “I guess you could say for that particular purpose, for the purpose of allowing a man who was thinking he was going to be in prison for life, out,” the US president told reporters in the East Room.

Witkoff also said that his discussions with Putin were “constructive”, and“will continue with trilateral talks between the United States, Russia and Ukraine at the technical level”. This comes after Trump’s reignited feud with Zelenskyy after he urged Kyiv to end its attacks on Russian refineries and waived sweeping sanctions against Moscow.

New polling from the New York Times and Siena University shows thatlikely voters prefer Democratic candidates over Republicans running for office by 11 percentage points. Meanwhile, Trump’s approval rating dropped to a new low for this particular survey – 36%.

At a campaign rally in Cincinnati, Ohio, JD Vance criticized the media and Democrats for focusing on Vivek Ramaswamy’s recent ad for his gubernatorial campaign, which features the estranged mother of his Democratic opponent,Amy Acton. The vice-president defended Ramaswamy for having “the audacity to run a TV commercial which calls it out like it is, and calls Amy Acton a liar”. Donna Arthur, Acton’s mother, claimed in the spot that her daughter “lied her entire life” about living in a tent during her childhood. However, Acton’s brother, Philip Stearns, said on Tuesday that his sister is estranged from her mother, who had married a man that sexually abused Acton when she was 12 years old. Arthur, he said, remained in the marriage even after her husband was arrested and her children were taken away from her.

The supreme court has refused to allow the Trump administration to immediately deny gender-affirming care for transgender people in federal prisons. The decision leaves in place a lower-court block on the policy while a legal challenge plays out. It was adopted after an executive order from Trump, who’s taken several steps to roll back transgender rights during his second term.

With 13 days until the midterms,Trump will continue his campaign blitz by heading to Clemson, South Carolina, where he’ll rally for Darline Graham – the Republican nominee for US Senate who is hoping to secure a full term for her late brother’s seat. Darline was appointed by the South Carolina governor to carry out the remainder of Lindsey Graham’s time in office after his death in July. However, she now faces a competitive race against Annie Andrews, a pediatrician and the Democratic nominee, in a contest that has become increasingly rancorous in recent months.
Trump defends special envoy Witkoff calling Putin a 'humanitarian'
In the East Room today, Trump defended Steve Witkoff’s comments, noting that the release of Steven Hubbard might warrant praise for Putin.
“I guess you could say for that particular purpose, for the purpose of allowing a man who was thinking he was going to be in prison for life, out,” Trump told reporters.

Earlier, we noted that Thom Tillis, the outgoing Republican senator from North Carolina, slammed special envoy Steve Witkoff for calling Vladimir Putin a “humanitarian” today – following the release of detained US citizen Steven Hubbard.
Now, more GOP lawmakers are pushing back.
“Vladimir Putin is not our friend, and he is certainly no humanitarian,” said retiring Republican senator Joni Ernst.
She added: “His relentless attacks on innocent civilians in Ukraine show his total disregard for human life. Appeasement won’t end this war. Pressure will.”

With 13 days until the midterms, early voting data is rolling in nationwide. Democrats need to net four Senate seats and hold 218 House seats to reclaim a congressional majority. Here is where the numbers stand so far:

Turnout is surging in key battlegrounds: Over 16 million Americans have already voted in person or by mail. According to the University of Florida’s Election Lab, battleground states -including Michigan, Ohio, Georgia, Texas, Florida and North Carolina – have each passed 700,000 ballots cast as of 21 October. Turnout is being driven in part by widespread voter frustration, reflected in Donald Trump’s record-low approval ratings.

Democrats lead in early returns: Registered Democrats account for 47% of early ballots cast, compared with 29% from Republicans (tracking returned ballots, not candidate selection). The party gap is most pronounced in North Carolina, Kansas and Iowa. While Republicans traditionally favor election day voting, strategists worry this widened margin signals a “red undertow” – GOP voters staying home due to frustration over high gas prices, the conflict in Iran and sweeping tariffs.

Early votes are pacing well ahead of 2022: In Georgia, early votes already represent nearly 30% of the total turnout from the 2022 midterms. Florida sits at 18%, with similarly high paces recorded in North Carolina, Michigan and Ohio.

Mail-in voting remains resilient: Over 56m mail-in ballots have been requested or sent nationally – greater than the 52m requested in 2022, according to NBC News (using data from TargetSmart). Despite executive orders from the Trump administration attempting to restrict mail-in voting, which the supreme court struck down in September, voters continue to utilize the process at pre-pandemic rates.
Meta ordered to pay $25bn penalty over deceiving users about data privacy

A judge in New Mexico ordered Meta to pay $25bn in penalties, on after a jury found the company had misled consumers in a case arising from allegations that Cambridge Analytica – a political consulting firm involved in Donald Trump’s 2016 presidential campaign – obtained data from millions of Facebook users without their consent.

The state’s attorney general had sued Meta in 2021 following revelations that Cambridge Analytica, a British political consulting firm, had harvested personal data from as many as 87 million Facebook users through a third-party app.

“Facebook’s wrongdoing – over the course of years and systematically broadcast to the public – goes to the heart of Facebook’s core business practices,” Judge Francis Mathew wrote in his order following the verdict.
Mathew found that a penalty of more than $219bn was warranted, based on state law, but he reduced the figure to $25bn.

In Maine, Susan Collins, the moderate Republican incumbent senator vying for a sixth term in office, joined the growing list of GOP lawmakers to urge the Trump administration to reverse the waiving of Russian sanctions.

“First of all the law is very clear, that we wanted additional sanctions to be imposed on Russia, by cutting the deal on diesel with Russia. [Trump] is not going to increase the supply to the United States in any measurable way. But what he is going to do is to get more funding for Russia to use to attack Ukraine,” Collins told reporters in Lewiston, where she was joined by former independent senator Joe Manchin for a campaign stop.
Vance criticizes outrage over Ramaswamy ad featuring opponent's estranged mother

At a campaign rally in Cincinnati, Ohio, JD Vance criticized the media and Democrats for focusing on Vivek Ramaswamy’s recent ad for his gubernatorial campaign, which features the estranged mother of his Democratic opponent, Amy Acton.

As we noted earlier, the campaign spot, which has circulated among conservatives on social media, shows Donna Arthur, Acton’s mother, claiming that her daughter “lied her entire life” about spending time living in a tent during her childhood.

However, Acton’s brother, Philip Stearns, blasted the ad, and said his sister is estranged from her mother, who had married a man that sexually abused Acton when she was 12 years old. Arthur, he said, remained in the marriage even after her husband was arrested and her children were taken away from her.
Today, Vance defended Ramaswamy for having “the audacity to run a TV commercial which calls it out like it isand calls Amy Acton a liar”.
Vance added: “My message, ladies and gentlemen, is very simple. Whatever you think about any of the TV advertisements, focus on the substance and focus on the facts.”
Witkoff calls meeting with Putin 'constructive', says trilateral talks will continue 'at the technical level'

Special envoy Steve Witkoff said his meeting today with Vladimir Putin – which resulted in the release of Stephen Hubbard, a 74-year-old former teacher who had spent more than four years in Russian jails– was “constructive”.

Trump’s emissary met with Russian leadership in St Petersburg, after talks in Oslo with Zelenskyy and Nordic leaders. The Ukrainian president has pushed for an in-person meeting with Moscow and Washington to hammer out a lasting peace deal, as fighting rages on.
Witkoff added that his discussions today “will continue with trilateral talks between the United States, Russia and Ukraine at the technical level”.

“While there is still important work left to do, President Trump remains committed to seeing this war end and achieving a comprehensive, durable peace that will provide security and prosperity for generations to come,” Witkoff said, following the president’s reignited feud with Zelenskyy after he urged Kyiv to end its attacks on Russian refineries and waived sweeping sanctions against Moscow.
A 24-year-old Kansas man has been arrested for allegedly threatening to shoot Donald Trump.

Authorities arrested Jaden J Read, of Clearwater, Kansas, last Saturday after he allegedly posted threats to kill the US president at his rally in the Wichita area on Monday, according to the justice department.

According to federal authorities, a Crime Stoppers tip on 15 October led investigators to a Facebook post responding to a KAKE News article about Trump’s upcoming Wichita visit. Read allegedly commented: “Let’s shoot Trump honestly, where’s our shooter? I’m tired of living this money life.”
Immediately afterward, he allegedly posted a second comment on the same article: “I just got a 308 and 305 round and I’m killing this pedo.”
Authorities also found two additional comments allegedly posted by Read in response to a KWCH 12 News article about Trump’s planned visit.

“Can we shoot him in Kansas please I will myself,” Read allegedly wrote. A minute later, he allegedly posted another comment, saying: “IK where your speech will be. Already mapped out roofs around. Finna get kirked since yall couldn’t help him.”

Read was arrested in Clearwater last Saturday and taken into federal custody, where he will remain pending a detention hearing. The district of Kansas filed a criminal complaint against Read for making threats against the president.
Retiring GOP senator Thom Tillis has ridiculed DonaldTrump’s special envoy Steve Witkoff for praising Vladimir Putinas a “humanitarian”.
“WTF, Steve? Look up the definition of ‘humanitarian,’” Tillis said in a post on X, with a screenshot showing the definition.

“What an embarrassing and outrageous thing to say,” the North Carolina senator went on. “You should go back to Ukraine and ask the families of the children Putin has kidnapped and murdered whether they agree your friend Putin is a ‘humanitarian.’”

Elena Kagan criticized rulings made by the US supreme court’s conservative majority this week, arguing that its recent decisions on redistricting and campaign finance had undermined America’s democracy.

“The court has kind of blinded itself to the very deleterious effects of their rulings on how the political system works,” said Kagan, one of the court’s three liberal justices, during a discussion at Catholic University’s law school in Washington DC yesterday, according to multiple reports.
She emphasized that the court, which has a 6-3 conservative majority, “has created a democracy that does not work as well as it should”.

Kagan’s remarks come just two weeks before the midterm elections and amid battles over congressional redistricting. Earlier this year, the supreme court struck down Louisiana’s congressional map, effectively gutting a major section of the Voting Rights Act. In June, the court also struck down campaign finance restrictions limiting how much political parties may spend on candidates. Both decisions were split 6-3 along ideological lines.

As a result, she said, “both political parties have been engaged in a race to the bottom in terms of doing these partisan gerrymanders, effectively depriving masses of citizens of their rights to voting equality”.
Kagan said that decision was pushing political candidates “away from the center, toward the wings, toward the extremes, because the only thing anybody has to worry about any more is being primaried”.

“It is making what I think is unfortunately a too polarized country even more so,” she continued. “In this election, and the next election, we are seeing large states with substantial numbers of people who vote for Republicans and who vote for Democrats, and the states are going to be tried to turn all red or all blue in a way that I think is very destructive to our democracy.”
Kagan also criticized the court’s decisions on campaign finance rules, and the increasing amounts of money in politics.
The people of America look around this political system and think that all this money chasing all these political candidates is a nightmare. And they’re right.
Supreme court rebuffs Trump restrictions on medical care for trans inmates for now
The supreme court has refused to allow the Trump administration to immediately deny gender-affirming care for transgender people in federal prisons.

The decision leaves in place a lower-court block on the policy while a legal challenge plays out. It was adopted after an executive order from Donald Trump, who’s taken several steps to roll back transgender rights during his second term.
Two of the supreme court’s six conservative justices, Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas, dissented, meaning they would have allowed the policy to be enforced.

Trump’s January 2025 executive order called on the Bureau of Prisons to revise its medical care policies so federal funds aren’t spent “for the purpose of conforming an inmate’s appearance to that of the opposite sex”.
The new policy would halt surgical and hormonal treatments, and end “social accommodations” like makeup and wigs. Prisons would continue to offer mental health services.
Trans prisoners sued the administration over the policy and, so far, two lower courts have blocked officials from implementing the order as the larger lawsuit over the executive order continues.
Steve Witkoff lavished praise on Vladimir Putin during their meeting at the grand Constantine Palace in St Petersburg, describing the Russian president as a humanitarian.

“You talk so much about my president, President Trump, being a humanitarian. You are a humanitarian also, sir, and I salute that,” Trump’s special envoy told Putin. He also conveyed Trump’s thanks for a deal to resume Russian diesel exports to the US.

The Russian president is wanted by the international criminal court (ICC) as a war criminal, in relation to the deportation of Ukrainian children to Russia during the war. More than 17,500 civilians have been confirmed killed in Ukraine since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022, according to the UN, which says the true toll is likely to be significantly higher.

The warmth of Witkoff’s remarks stood in stark contrast to the increasingly hostile rhetoric directed at Volodymyr Zelenskyy by senior US officials, most notably Trump, who has called for the Ukrainian president to resign and portrayed him as the main obstacle to peace.

Witkoff travelled to Russia from Oslo, where he had met Zelenskyy and European leaders a day earlier in an attempt to inject momentum into stalled negotiations, with Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine now in its fifth year.
Witkoff told Putin during a televised portion of their meeting:
We’ve brought some papers. It’s really some ideas, some sort of peace deal between Russia and Ukraine, and you’ll read that at your leisure.
The visit was Witkoff’s ninth to Russia since Trump tasked him with brokering an end to the war.
A White House official has confirmed to the Guardian that Donald Trump’s roundtable at 2.30pm ET will be focused on cybercrime.

The president is “unleashing every available tool to stop foreign-based organized criminal organizations that exploit Americans in cyberspace”, the official said in a statement. “The most vulnerable among us – seniors, children, and low-income families – are disproportionately targeted, with scammers draining life savings, stealing the benefits of years of work, and destroying lives.”
According to the FBI, Americans reported losing almost $21bn to cybercrime and internet scams.
While Donald Trump will be in South Carolina today, his vice-president, JD Vance, will be stumping in Cincinnati, Ohio.

The Buckeye state is home to a must-keep Senate seat for Republicans, where the incumbent, John Husted, is fending off a challenge from former Democratic senator Sherrod Brown – the populist hoping for a comeback.

The state’s gubernatorial competition has also become increasingly bitter. On Tuesday, my colleague Chris Stein reported that the family of Amy Acton, the Democratic candidate for governor of Ohio, is criticizing her Republican opponent Vivek Ramaswamy for using Acton’s estranged mother in a recently released campaign ad.
In the ad, which has circulated among conservatives on social media, Actons’s mother, Donna Arthur, said: “She says she grew up living in a tent. None of that is true. She’s lied her entire life.”

In a Tuesday statement, Acton’s brother, Philip Stearns, said his sister is estranged from her mother, who had married a man that sexually abused Acton when she was 12 years old. He added that Arthur remained in the marriage even after her husband was arrested and her children were taken away from her.

“It’s not surprising that Vivek Ramaswamy has stooped to such a despicable low as to attempt to turn the sexual abuse Amy endured at twelve years old from our birth mother’s husband into a political talking point,” he said in a statement released by Acton’s campaign.
Trump praises UK approval of controversial Jackdaw gasfield in North Sea
Donald Trump has welcomed the news that UK government has approved the controversial Jackdaw gasfield in the North Sea.

“Great news for the wealth and prosperity of the United Kingdom, and the wonderful region of Aberdeen. The UK has started drilling in the North Sea, one of the greatest and most prosperous areas of OIL in the World,” the US president wrote on Truth Social.
He added that the UK should go “FULL BLAST”, and the move to resume offshore extraction would “make the UK very wealthy again”.

As my colleagues reported earlier today, Andy Burnham, the UK prime minister, said the Jackdaw project will “protect hundreds of jobs and help keep millions of homes warm this winter”. This comes after fierce opposition from several Labour MPs and environmental groups throughout the country.

Trump has long pushed for Britain to expand oil and gas drilling in the North Sea, instead of relying on wind turbines. He frequently clashed with Burnham’s predecessor, Keir Starmer, who argued that energy sustainability relied on renewable sources and moving away from fossil fuel dependence.

articles.headline: EA cancels unannounced The Sims project, trims the Skate team and reportedly plans to lay off 400 workers: "We're the number one publisher in Western HD gaming"
keyFacts: Electronic Arts announced plans to cut 400 jobs and close BioWare while pausing development on an unannounced Sims project.
Executives David Tinson and Cam Weber stated in a staff memo that the changes are due to a rapidly changing industry.
EA will now focus on fewer large-scale projects while continuing work on franchises like Apex Legends and Battlefield.
body: Not only is EA closing down BioWare and cancelling the next Mass Effect - Electronic Arts has now announced a heap of drastic changes that include cutting 400 jobs across the company, pausing development on a project connected to The Sims, and bringing together Respawn and DICE.
In a memo first sent to staff and later published online, CEO David Tinson and CSO Cam Weber first took a moment to thank employees before letting them know they might lose their jobs.

"Today, we're the number one publisher in Western HD gaming," the duo wrote. "That's an extraordinary position to lead from, and one we should be proud of. Yet our industry is changing quickly. Players have more choices than ever for their time and attention, competition is intensifying, and some of our biggest opportunities for growth are beyond the markets, platforms, and business models where EA has traditionally been the strongest."

The executives then laid out some changes to its portfolio of games. Top of the list is the closure of BioWare, the legendary role-playing powerhouse behind games such as Mass Effect and Dragon Age. Bloomberg reports around 400 jobs will be cut as part of the cost-cutting changes, including roughly 50 job cuts at BioWare.

As for The Sims, the publisher claims it's prioritising something called "Project Evergreen" and is giving "the team more time to reach the full potential and vision for the game." To do so, the execs said they're "pausing development" on another Sims-related title called "Project Lotus." The early access Skate reboot (skate.) has apparently "had a lot of success," but the publisher is still restructuring the studio into a "more focused, smaller team," regardless.

Marvel's Iron Man game (the one that leaked recently) and a third Star Wars Jedi game remain untouched, apparently, though it sounds like we'll see fewer big-budget action-adventure games come from the publisher going forward: "Beyond that, we will concentrate our efforts on fewer simultaneous, large-scale projects, ensuring that every game we build in this space is fully set up for success."

EA also re-emphasised its commitment to Apex Legends and the Battlefield series after the success of Battlefield 6. But that's not all. "We'll be bringing together our Respawn and DICE studios to collaborate on a future project." There's been some rumblings about a possible Star Wars: Battlefront follow-up this week, though EA doesn't give any more concrete details about what this game could be.

Then there's the publisher's golden goose, EA Sports. The executives said they're still committed to FC and the rest of its sport simulations, alongside two new projects that'll be revealed in the next few months - the return of Fight Night and a "brand-new, social-first open-world experience for our American Football team that we call 'Project Gridiron'".

"The decisions we’re making in our priorities, how we work, and with our portfolio reflect our belief in EA’s future. Some open exciting new possibilities. Others are difficult, especially for the people and teams across the company who are directly affected. In those cases, we will support impacted employees in exploring other opportunities within EA, and we're committed to treating impacted colleagues with care and respect," the executives added.
A group of investment firms led by Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund took EA private earlier this summer, in a deal worth around $55 billion.
